topic: Commercial privileges, limitations and operations for hire

notes.front: What is a letter of authorization (LOA) under §91.147?
notes.back: The authorization an operator of nonstop passenger-carrying flights for hire, beginning and ending at one airport within 25 statute miles, must apply for and receive.
notes.explanation: It is issued by the responsible Flight Standards office, and the operator must then comply with its provisions.
notes.example: Like a local trading permit for a sightseeing boat that leaves and returns to the same quay, rather than a full ferry-line licence.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.147 Passenger-carrying flights for compensation or hire (eCFR), paragraph (b)(4)
notes.evidence: Apply for and receive a Letter of Authorization from the responsible Flight Standards office.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What may the holder of a commercial pilot certificate act as pilot in command of an aircraft doing?
notes.back: Carrying persons or property for compensation or hire, and flying for compensation or hire.
notes.explanation: §61.133(a)(1) lists both, each on condition that the pilot is qualified for the operation.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.133 Commercial pilot privileges and limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)
notes.evidence: A person who holds a commercial pilot certificate may act as pilot in command of an aircraft— (i) Carrying persons or property for compensation or hire
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Besides carrying persons or property, a commercial pilot may act as pilot in command of an aircraft {{c1::for compensation or hire}}.
notes.explanation: The second privilege covers paid flying in which nobody and nothing is carried for hire.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.133 Commercial pilot privileges and limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)(ii)
notes.evidence: (ii) For compensation or hire, provided the person is qualified in accordance with this part and with the applicable parts of this chapter that apply to the operation.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What condition attaches to each commercial pilot privilege in §61.133(a)(1)?
notes.back: The pilot must be qualified under part 61 and under the other parts of the regulations that apply to the operation.
notes.explanation: The certificate alone is not the whole authority; the rules for the kind of operation apply as well.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.133 Commercial pilot privileges and limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)(i)
notes.evidence: provided the person is qualified in accordance with this part and with the applicable parts of this chapter that apply to the operation
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which commercial airplane applicants receive a certificate with a limitation on carrying passengers for hire?
notes.back: Those who do not hold an instrument rating in the same category and class.
notes.explanation: The limitation follows from the missing instrument rating, not from hours or experience.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.133 Commercial pilot privileges and limitations (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: does not hold an instrument rating in the same category and class will be issued a commercial pilot certificate that contains the limitation
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does the limitation on a commercial airplane certificate without an instrument rating prohibit?
notes.back: Carrying passengers for hire on cross-country flights of more than 50 nautical miles, or at night.
notes.explanation: It restricts passengers for hire; it does not bar other commercial flying.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.133 Commercial pilot privileges and limitations (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: “The carriage of passengers for hire in (airplanes) (powered-lifts) on cross-country flights in excess of 50 nautical miles or at night is prohibited.”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Without an instrument rating, a commercial pilot may not carry passengers for hire in airplanes on cross-country flights in excess of {{c1::50 nautical miles}}.
notes.explanation: The distance applies to cross-country flights; the same limitation also covers any flight at night.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.133 Commercial pilot privileges and limitations (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: The carriage of passengers for hire in (airplanes) (powered-lifts) on cross-country flights in excess of 50 nautical miles or at night is prohibited.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How may a commercial pilot have the no-instrument-rating limitation removed?
notes.back: By meeting the §61.65 requirements for an instrument rating in the same category and class as the commercial certificate.
notes.explanation: The limitation stays only as long as the instrument rating in that category and class is missing.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.133 Commercial pilot privileges and limitations (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: The limitation may be removed when the person satisfactorily accomplishes the requirements listed in § 61.65 of this part for an instrument rating in the same category and class of aircraft
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Part 119 applies to each person operating or intending to operate civil aircraft in which capacity, among others?
notes.back: As an air carrier or commercial operator, or both, in air commerce.
notes.explanation: Part 119 is where operators obtain the certificates for operations under parts 121, 125 and 135.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: This part applies to each person operating or intending to operate civil aircraft— (1) As an air carrier or commercial operator, or both, in air commerce; or
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What are two things part 119 prescribes?
notes.back: The types of air operator certificates; the requirements to obtain one for operations under parts 121, 125 or 135.
notes.explanation: These are the certificates a commercial operator needs beyond the pilot's own certificate.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: The types of air operator certificates issued by the Federal Aviation Administration, including air carrier certificates and operating certificates; (2) The certification requirements an operator must meet in order to obtain and hold a certificate authorizing operations under part 121, 125, or 135
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Operations under which parts does part 119 not govern, besides part 91 subpart K without common carriage?
notes.explanation: §119.1(d) names these parts alongside part 91 subpart K operations without common carriage.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (d)
notes.evidence: nor does it govern operations conducted under part 129, 133, 137, or 139 of this chapter.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For which operations do the §119.1(e) exceptions not apply?
notes.back: Operations without common carriage using an airplane with 20 or more passenger seats or a payload capacity of 6,000 pounds or more.
notes.explanation: Size brings an operation back under part 119 even when it would otherwise be on the list of exceptions.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)
notes.evidence: Except for operations when common carriage is not involved conducted with any airplane or powered-lift having a passenger-seat configuration of 20 seats or more, excluding any required crewmember seat, or a payload capacity of 6,000 pounds or more, this part does not apply to—
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Part 119 does not apply to {{c1::student instruction}}.
notes.explanation: It is the first operation on the §119.1(e) list, so paid flight training needs no operator certificate under part 119.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(1)
notes.evidence: this part does not apply to— (1) Student instruction;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: {{c1::Ferry or training}} flights are outside part 119.
notes.explanation: The item sits in the §119.1(e) list between the air tour exception and aerial work.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(3)
notes.evidence: (3) Ferry or training flights;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under which heading does §119.1(e) place crop dusting, banner towing and fire fighting?
notes.back: Aerial work operations.
notes.explanation: The heading says "including", so the items it names are examples of aerial work.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(4)
notes.evidence: (4) Aerial work operations, including— (i) Crop dusting, seeding, spraying, and bird chasing; (ii) Banner towing;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which §119.1(e)(4) aerial work item includes bird chasing?
notes.back: Crop dusting, seeding, spraying and bird chasing.
notes.explanation: Bird chasing is grouped with the agricultural work in the first item of the list.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(4)(i)
notes.evidence: (i) Crop dusting, seeding, spraying, and bird chasing;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which §119.1(e)(4) aerial work item covers mapping or photographing land from the air?
notes.back: Aerial photography or survey.
notes.explanation: Photography and survey share one item on the aerial work list.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(4)(iii)
notes.evidence: (iii) Aerial photography or survey;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which §119.1(e)(4) aerial work item covers flying along power lines or pipelines to inspect them?
notes.back: Powerline or pipeline patrol.
notes.explanation: It is the last named item of the aerial work list, after fire fighting and construction work.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(4)(vi)
notes.evidence: (vi) Powerline or pipeline patrol;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For powered-lift or rotorcraft construction or repair work, which part of the flying does part 119 still cover?
notes.back: Transportation to and from the site of operations.
notes.explanation: The work itself is excepted as aerial work, but carrying people or goods to the site is not.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(4)(v)
notes.evidence: Powered-lift or rotorcraft operations in construction or repair work (but part 119 of this chapter does apply to transportation to and from the site of operations);
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which nonstop commercial air tours are outside part 119?
notes.back: Those beginning and ending at the same airport, within a 25-statute-mile radius, under a §91.147 Letter of Authorization.
notes.explanation: All three conditions must hold, together with the aircraft limits on seats, payload and airworthiness certificate.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(2)
notes.evidence: that begin and end at the same airport, and are conducted within a 25-statute mile radius of that airport, in compliance with the Letter of Authorization issued under § 91.147 of this chapter.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What aircraft limits apply to the §119.1(e)(2) air tour exception?
notes.back: A standard airworthiness certificate, 30 passenger seats or fewer, and a maximum payload capacity of 7,500 pounds or less.
notes.explanation: They are set inside the air tour item itself; the 20-seat and 6,000-pound test in the opening words of §119.1(e) is separate and covers every item, air tours included, when common carriage is not involved.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(2)
notes.evidence: having a standard airworthiness certificate and passenger-seat configuration of 30 seats or fewer and a maximum payload capacity of 7,500 pounds or less
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Do the requirements of part 119 apply to nonstop commercial air tours conducted under part 136, subpart B (National Parks Air Tour Management)?
notes.back: Yes, unless excepted in §136.37(g)(2).
notes.explanation: National park tours are carved back out of the air tour exception.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(2)
notes.evidence: For nonstop Commercial Air Tours conducted in accordance with part 136, subpart B, of this chapter, National Parks Air Tour Management, the requirements of this part apply unless excepted in § 136.37(g)(2).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which parachute flights are outside part 119?
notes.back: Nonstop flights within a 25-statute-mile radius of the takeoff airport, carrying persons or objects for intentional parachute operations.
notes.explanation: The same 25-statute-mile radius appears in the air tour exception.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(6)
notes.evidence: Nonstop flights conducted within a 25-statute-mile radius of the airport of takeoff carrying persons or objects for the purpose of conducting intentional parachute operations.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In which aircraft are sightseeing flights outside part 119?
notes.back: Hot air balloons and gliders.
notes.explanation: Sightseeing in an airplane is not on this item; it escapes part 119 only as a nonstop air tour meeting §119.1(e)(2).
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(5)
notes.evidence: (5) Sightseeing flights conducted in hot air balloons or gliders;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Who is an "Operator" for the purposes of §91.147?
notes.back: Anyone conducting nonstop passenger-carrying flights for hire in an airplane, powered-lift or rotorcraft, beginning and ending at one airport within 25 statute miles.
notes.explanation: The definition matches the air tour exception in §119.1(e)(2), which the section cites.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.147 Passenger-carrying flights for compensation or hire (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: Operator means any person conducting nonstop passenger-carrying flights in an airplane, powered-lift, or rotorcraft for compensation or hire in accordance with §§ 119.1(e)(2), 135.1(a)(5), or 121.1(d) of this chapter that begin and end at the same airport and are conducted within a 25-statute mile radius of that airport.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: From whom does a §91.147 Operator apply for and receive its Letter of Authorization?
notes.back: The responsible Flight Standards office.
notes.explanation: Receiving the letter is one of the four general requirements the Operator must meet.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.147 Passenger-carrying flights for compensation or hire (eCFR), paragraph (b)(4)
notes.evidence: Apply for and receive a Letter of Authorization from the responsible Flight Standards office.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Whose safety provisions must a §91.147 Operator comply with?
notes.back: Those of part 136, subpart A.
notes.explanation: It is the first of four general requirements, before drug and alcohol testing, part 5 and the letter itself.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.147 Passenger-carrying flights for compensation or hire (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: Comply with the safety provisions of part 136, subpart A of this chapter.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What programmes must a §91.147 Operator register and implement under part 120?
notes.back: Drug and alcohol testing programmes.
notes.explanation: The application for the letter also asks for the antidrug and alcohol misuse prevention programme registration.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.147 Passenger-carrying flights for compensation or hire (eCFR), paragraph (b)(2)
notes.evidence: Register and implement its drug and alcohol testing programs in accordance with part 120 of this chapter.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A §91.147 Operator must comply with the applicable requirements of part {{c1::5}}.
notes.explanation: It is the third of the four general requirements, after part 136 and part 120.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.147 Passenger-carrying flights for compensation or hire (eCFR), paragraph (b)(3)
notes.evidence: Comply with the applicable requirements of part 5 of this chapter.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What are two items an application for a §91.147 Letter of Authorization must include?
notes.back: The name of the person responsible for aircraft maintenance; the type of aircraft and registration numbers.
notes.explanation: The application lists seven items, among them business addresses and the management and maintenance contacts.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.147 Passenger-carrying flights for compensation or hire (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: (5) Name of person responsible for aircraft maintenance. (6) Type of aircraft, registration number(s), and make/model/series.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does the commercial airplane Airman Certification Standards require applicants to know about special airworthiness certificates?
notes.back: The operating limitations of aircraft with special airworthiness certificates, where applicable.
notes.explanation: It sits in the Airworthiness Requirements task of the first area of operation, with a note that it applies where relevant.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation I, Task B, knowledge element K4
notes.evidence: Special airworthiness certificate aircraft operating limitations, if applicable.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For what may a restricted category civil aircraft be operated?
notes.back: Only for the special purpose for which it is certificated, and operations necessary for the work directly associated with it.
notes.explanation: The later ban on carriage for hire builds on this limit to the special purpose.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.313 Restricted category civil aircraft: Operating limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: No person may operate a restricted category civil aircraft— (1) For other than the special purpose for which it is certificated; or (2) In an operation other than one necessary to accomplish the work activity directly associated with that special purpose.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: May a restricted category civil aircraft carry persons or property for compensation or hire?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Carrying persons or material needed for the special purpose itself is not counted as carriage for hire.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.313 Restricted category civil aircraft: Operating limitations (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: No person may operate a restricted category civil aircraft carrying persons or property for compensation or hire. For the purposes of this paragraph (c), a special purpose operation involving the carriage of persons or material necessary to accomplish that operation
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which carriage in a restricted category aircraft is not considered carriage for compensation or hire?
notes.back: Persons or material necessary for its special purpose operation, such as crop dusting or banner towing.
notes.explanation: The regulation also names crewmember training for the special purpose as outside the ban.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.313 Restricted category civil aircraft: Operating limitations (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: a special purpose operation involving the carriage of persons or material necessary to accomplish that operation, such as crop dusting, seeding, spraying, and banner towing
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In which operations may a limited category civil aircraft not carry persons or property for hire? Name two.
notes.back: Operations requiring a part 119 certificate; operations listed in §119.1(e).
notes.explanation: The list also covers fractional ownership programmes and operations under parts 129, 133 and 137.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.315 Limited category civil aircraft: Operating limitations (eCFR)
notes.evidence: no person may operate a limited category civil aircraft carrying persons or property for compensation or hire in operations that: (a) Require an air carrier or commercial operator certificate issued under part 119 of this chapter; (b) Are listed in § 119.1(e) of this chapter;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What two limits does §91.319(a) place on operating an aircraft with an experimental certificate?
notes.back: Only for the purpose the certificate was issued for; and no persons or property for hire in the listed operations.
notes.explanation: The listed operations include those needing a part 119 certificate and those in §119.1(e).
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.319 Aircraft having experimental certificates: Operating limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: no person may operate an aircraft that has an experimental airworthiness certificate— (1) For other than the purpose for which the certificate was issued; or (2) Carrying persons or property for compensation or hire in operations that:
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An experimental aircraft may not carry persons or property for hire in operations that require a part 119 certificate or that are listed in {{c1::§119.1(e)}}.
notes.explanation: So even the operations excepted from part 119, such as aerial work, are closed to experimental aircraft carrying for hire.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.319 Aircraft having experimental certificates: Operating limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)
notes.evidence: (i) Require an air carrier or commercial operator certificate issued under part 119 of this chapter; (ii) Are listed in § 119.1(e) of this chapter;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For which training activities may a light-sport category aircraft be operated for compensation or hire?
notes.back: Flight training, checking and testing.
notes.explanation: It is one of only three purposes for which the light-sport category allows operation for hire.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.327 Aircraft issued a special airworthiness certificate in the light-sport category: Operating limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)
notes.evidence: To conduct flight training, checking, and testing; or
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What towing may a light-sport category aircraft do for compensation or hire?
notes.back: Glider or unpowered ultralight vehicle towing, as specified in its handbook or operating limitations and statement of compliance.
notes.explanation: The towing must be provided for in the aircraft's own documents.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.327 Aircraft issued a special airworthiness certificate in the light-sport category: Operating limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)
notes.evidence: To conduct any glider or an unpowered ultralight vehicle towing operations in accordance with § 91.309, that are specified in the aircraft's pilot operating handbook or operating limitations
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which aerial work may a light-sport category aircraft do for compensation or hire?
notes.back: Aerial work operations specified in its pilot operating handbook or operating limitations and in the manufacturer's statement of compliance.
notes.explanation: As with towing, the work must be specified in the aircraft's documents.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.327 Aircraft issued a special airworthiness certificate in the light-sport category: Operating limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(3)
notes.evidence: To conduct any aerial work operations specified in the aircraft's pilot operating handbook or operating limitations, as applicable, and specified in the manufacturer's statement of compliance
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What inspection must an aircraft carrying any person other than a crewmember for hire have had within the preceding 100 hours of time in service?
notes.back: An annual or 100-hour inspection, with approval for return to service (or an inspection for an airworthiness certificate).
notes.explanation: Carrying people for hire adds this time-in-service limit to the annual inspection every aircraft needs.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.409 Inspections (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: no person may operate an aircraft carrying any person (other than a crewmember) for hire, and no person may give flight instruction for hire in an aircraft which that person provides, unless within the preceding 100 hours of time in service the aircraft has received an annual or 100-hour inspection
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Besides carrying persons for hire, what activity brings an aircraft under the 100-hour inspection rule?
notes.back: Giving flight instruction for hire in an aircraft that the instructor provides.
notes.explanation: An aircraft the student provides is not caught by this part of the rule.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.409 Inspections (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: no person may give flight instruction for hire in an aircraft which that person provides
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: By how much may the 100-hour limit be exceeded, and for what purpose?
notes.back: By not more than 10 hours, while en route to reach a place where the inspection can be done.
notes.explanation: The margin is only for the flight to where the inspection can be done.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.409 Inspections (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: The 100-hour limitation may be exceeded by not more than 10 hours while en route to reach a place where the inspection can be done.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How is time flown beyond 100 hours to reach an inspection treated?
notes.back: It is included in computing the next 100 hours of time in service.
notes.explanation: The extra time is borrowed from the next interval, not added free.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.409 Inspections (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: The excess time used to reach a place where the inspection can be done must be included in computing the next 100 hours of time in service.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Lena holds a commercial certificate without an instrument rating. She is paid to fly two passengers on a daytime cross-country of 40 nautical miles. Does the limitation stop her?
notes.back: B) No: the flight is by day and not in excess of 50 nautical miles
notes.choices:
A) Yes: no passengers for hire at all
B) No: the flight is by day and not in excess of 50 nautical miles
C) Yes: cross-country flights are banned
D) No: the limitation applies only to cargo
notes.choicesExplained: A and C overstate the limitation. D: it concerns passengers for hire, not cargo.
notes.explanation: The limitation bites only beyond 50 nautical miles or at night.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.133 Commercial pilot privileges and limitations (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: The carriage of passengers for hire in (airplanes) (powered-lifts) on cross-country flights in excess of 50 nautical miles or at night is prohibited.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Lena, still without an instrument rating, is offered pay to fly a passenger on a daytime cross-country of 80 nautical miles. May she?
notes.back: B) No: it is a cross-country in excess of 50 nautical miles
notes.choices:
A) Yes: it is daytime
B) No: it is a cross-country in excess of 50 nautical miles
C) Yes, if the weather is good VFR
D) Yes, if the passenger shares the costs pro rata
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: daylight and good weather do not lift the distance limit. D: this is a flight for hire, which the limitation covers.
notes.explanation: The distance limit applies to passenger-carrying cross-countries whatever the weather.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.133 Commercial pilot privileges and limitations (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: The carriage of passengers for hire in (airplanes) (powered-lifts) on cross-country flights in excess of 50 nautical miles or at night is prohibited.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A commercial pilot without an instrument rating is asked to fly a paying passenger on a 20-minute local flight after dark. May she?
notes.back: B) No: carriage of passengers for hire at night is prohibited
notes.choices:
A) Yes: it is not a cross-country
B) No: carriage of passengers for hire at night is prohibited
C) Yes: the limit is 50 nautical miles
D) Yes, with a flight instructor on board
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the night part of the limitation applies whatever the distance. D: the limitation has no instructor exception.
notes.explanation: The limitation has two limbs, and night is one of them on its own.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.133 Commercial pilot privileges and limitations (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: The carriage of passengers for hire in (airplanes) (powered-lifts) on cross-country flights in excess of 50 nautical miles or at night is prohibited.

B) No: the limitation concerns only the carriage of passengers for hire

notes.front: Tom, a private pilot, is offered pay by a local business to fly a parcel to another town. Which certificate would let him act as pilot in command of that flight, if he is qualified for the operation?
notes.back: C) A commercial pilot certificate
notes.choices:
A) His private pilot certificate
B) A student pilot certificate
C) A commercial pilot certificate
D) No pilot certificate allows it
notes.choicesExplained: A: a private pilot may not carry property for hire. B: a student certificate carries fewer privileges than a private one. D: the commercial certificate allows it.
notes.explanation: Carrying property for compensation or hire is the commercial pilot's privilege.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.133 Commercial pilot privileges and limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)
notes.evidence: A person who holds a commercial pilot certificate may act as pilot in command of an aircraft— (i) Carrying persons or property for compensation or hire
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A newly certificated commercial pilot plans to sell seats on flights between two cities as his own business. Is the commercial pilot certificate enough?
notes.back: B) No: he must also be qualified under the parts that apply to the operation, such as part 119 for an air carrier
notes.choices:
A) Yes: it allows carrying persons for hire
B) No: he must also be qualified under the parts that apply to the operation, such as part 119 for an air carrier
C) Yes, if he holds a second-class medical
D) Yes, if the flights stay within 50 nautical miles
notes.choicesExplained: A: the privilege is conditional. C: the medical is needed but is not the whole answer. D: no distance limit takes an air carrier's flights outside part 119.
notes.explanation: The privilege holds only when the pilot is qualified under the parts that apply to the operation, and part 119 applies to air carriers.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.133 Commercial pilot privileges and limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(1)(i)
notes.evidence: provided the person is qualified in accordance with this part and with the applicable parts of this chapter that apply to the operation
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A company intends to operate civil aircraft as an air carrier in air commerce. Which part prescribes the certificate it needs?
notes.back: C) Part 119
notes.choices:
A) Part 61
B) Part 91
C) Part 119
D) Part 43
notes.choicesExplained: A: part 61 certificates pilots, not operators. B: part 91 holds general operating rules. D: part 43 covers maintenance.
notes.explanation: Part 119 applies to air carriers and commercial operators and prescribes their certificates.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: This part applies to each person operating or intending to operate civil aircraft— (1) As an air carrier or commercial operator, or both, in air commerce; or
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A flight school charges students for dual lessons in its airplanes. Does part 119 apply to these lessons?
notes.back: B) No: student instruction is excepted
notes.choices:
A) Yes: money changes hands
B) No: student instruction is excepted
C) Yes, unless the airplane is a TAA
D) No, but only in daylight

notes.evidence: this part does not apply to— (1) Student instruction;

notes.front: A commercial pilot is paid to ferry an empty airplane from a dealer to its new owner. Does part 119 apply to the flight?
notes.back: B) No: ferry flights are excepted
notes.choices:
A) Yes: the pilot is paid
B) No: ferry flights are excepted
C) Yes: it is air commerce
D) No, but only if it is under 25 statute miles
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: payment does not remove the exception. D: the 25-statute-mile limit belongs to air tours and parachute flights.
notes.explanation: Ferry flights are on the §119.1(e) list with no distance limit.

notes.front: A commercial pilot is paid to tow an advertising banner along a beach. How does part 119 treat the flight?
notes.back: B) It is aerial work, which part 119 does not apply to
notes.choices:
A) It needs an air carrier certificate
B) It is aerial work, which part 119 does not apply to
C) It is an air tour needing a Letter of Authorization
D) It is student instruction
notes.choicesExplained: A: banner towing is excepted. C: no passengers are carried on a tour. D: nobody is being taught.
notes.explanation: Banner towing is listed as aerial work in §119.1(e)(4).
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(4)
notes.evidence: (4) Aerial work operations, including— (i) Crop dusting, seeding, spraying, and bird chasing; (ii) Banner towing;

notes.front: An estate agent pays a commercial pilot to photograph farms from the air. Which §119.1(e) exception applies?
notes.back: A) Aerial work: aerial photography or survey
notes.choices:
A) Aerial work: aerial photography or survey
B) Student instruction
C) Ferry flights
D) None: it needs a part 119 certificate
notes.choicesExplained: B and C describe other flights. D: aerial photography is on the aerial work list.

notes.front: An energy company pays a commercial pilot to fly along its pipeline looking for leaks. Is this within a §119.1(e) exception?
notes.back: A) Yes: powerline or pipeline patrol is aerial work
notes.choices:
A) Yes: powerline or pipeline patrol is aerial work
B) No: it needs an air carrier certificate
C) Only within 25 statute miles of the airport
D) Only with a Letter of Authorization
notes.choicesExplained: B: patrol is excepted. C and D are conditions of the air tour exception, not of aerial work.
notes.explanation: Pipeline patrol is named in the aerial work item of the list.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(4)(vi)

notes.front: An operator flies paying sightseers on nonstop airplane tours that return to the departure airport and stay within 20 statute miles. It holds a §91.147 Letter of Authorization. Does part 119 apply?
notes.back: B) No: this is the §119.1(e)(2) air tour exception
notes.choices:
A) Yes: passengers pay
B) No: this is the §119.1(e)(2) air tour exception
C) Yes: tours always need part 119
D) No, but only with gliders
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the exception exists for exactly this case. D: the glider item concerns sightseeing in balloons and gliders, not airplanes.
notes.explanation: The flights meet each condition: nonstop, the same airport, within 25 statute miles and under the letter.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(2)
notes.evidence: that begin and end at the same airport, and are conducted within a 25-statute mile radius of that airport, in compliance with the Letter of Authorization issued under § 91.147 of this chapter.

notes.front: The same operator wants a tour that reaches a lake 40 statute miles from the departure airport before returning nonstop. Is it still within the air tour exception?
notes.back: B) No: it goes beyond the 25-statute-mile radius
notes.choices:
A) Yes: it is nonstop and returns to the same airport
B) No: it goes beyond the 25-statute-mile radius
C) Yes, if the Letter of Authorization names the lake
D) No: tours must stay within 10 statute miles
notes.choicesExplained: A: every condition must be met, including the radius. C: the letter cannot extend the radius in §119.1(e)(2). D: the radius is 25 statute miles.
notes.explanation: The exception is tied to a 25-statute-mile radius of the airport.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(2)
notes.evidence: that begin and end at the same airport, and are conducted within a 25-statute mile radius of that airport, in compliance with the Letter of Authorization issued under § 91.147 of this chapter.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

A) Nothing: the flights are under 25 statute miles
B) A Letter of Authorization from the responsible Flight Standards office

D) A flight instructor certificate

notes.front: The owner of a restricted category crop duster is offered money to give a friend of a farmer a ride to a town 50 miles away. May he?
notes.back: B) No: a restricted category aircraft may not carry persons for compensation or hire
notes.choices:
A) Yes, with a commercial certificate
B) No: a restricted category aircraft may not carry persons for compensation or hire
C) Yes, if it has had a 100-hour inspection
D) Yes, if the flight is under 25 statute miles
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: pilot certificate and inspections do not lift the category limit. D: there is no distance exception.
notes.explanation: The ride has nothing to do with the special purpose, so it is carriage for hire.

notes.front: A pilot who built an experimental airplane is offered payment to fly a passenger on a scenic tour. Which rule stops it?
notes.back: B) §91.319: no persons for hire in operations that need part 119 or are listed in §119.1(e)
notes.choices:
A) None: the pilot holds a commercial certificate
B) §91.319: no persons for hire in operations that need part 119 or are listed in §119.1(e)
C) §61.133(b): the 50 nautical mile limit
D) §91.409: the 100-hour inspection
notes.choicesExplained: A: the pilot's certificate does not change the aircraft's limits. C: that limitation depends on the pilot, not the aircraft. D: an inspection would not make the flight lawful.
notes.explanation: A scenic tour for hire is either a part 119 operation or on the §119.1(e) list, and both are closed to experimental aircraft.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.319 Aircraft having experimental certificates: Operating limitations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)
notes.evidence: Carrying persons or property for compensation or hire in operations that: (i) Require an air carrier or commercial operator certificate issued under part 119 of this chapter; (ii) Are listed in § 119.1(e) of this chapter;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.back: C) Paid lessons only
notes.choices:
A) Both

D) Paid sightseeing only

notes.front: An airplane had its annual inspection four months ago and has flown 104 hours since. A commercial pilot is booked to fly paying passengers in it. May the flight go?
notes.back: B) No: carrying persons for hire needs an annual or 100-hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours
notes.choices:
A) Yes: the annual is current
B) No: carrying persons for hire needs an annual or 100-hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours
C) Yes: 10 hours of overrun are always allowed
D) Yes, if the passengers are crewmembers
notes.choicesExplained: A: the annual alone does not satisfy the hourly limit. C: the 10 hours are only for reaching a place of inspection. D: paying passengers are not crewmembers.
notes.explanation: With persons carried for hire, the inspection must fall within the last 100 hours of time in service.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.409 Inspections (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: no person may operate an aircraft carrying any person (other than a crewmember) for hire, and no person may give flight instruction for hire in an aircraft which that person provides, unless within the preceding 100 hours of time in service the aircraft has received an annual or 100-hour inspection
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A charter airplane reaches 100 hours since its last inspection at an airport with no maintenance. The nearest shop is 3 hours' flying away. What does §91.409(b) allow?
notes.back: B) Up to 10 hours over while en route to where the inspection can be done
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: it is grounded
B) Up to 10 hours over while en route to where the inspection can be done
C) Up to 25 hours over
D) Unlimited time, if no passengers are carried
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule gives a margin for this case. C: the margin is 10 hours. D: the margin is capped.
notes.explanation: The 10-hour margin exists for reaching a place of inspection, and the time counts against the next 100.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.409 Inspections (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: The 100-hour limitation may be exceeded by not more than 10 hours while en route to reach a place where the inspection can be done.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does a private pilot certificate forbid that a commercial pilot certificate allows?
notes.back: Acting as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying passengers or property for compensation or hire, or for compensation or hire at all.
notes.explanation: The private ban has its own listed exceptions in §61.113(b) to (h); the commercial certificate lifts the general ban.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.113 Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: Except as provided in paragraphs (b) through (h) of this section, no person who holds a private pilot certificate may act as pilot in command of an aircraft that is carrying passengers or property for compensation or hire; nor may that person, for compensation or hire, act as pilot in command of an aircraft.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How do the air tour exception's own aircraft limits differ from the size test in the opening words of §119.1(e)?
notes.back: Air tours: 30 seats or fewer, 7,500 pounds or less. Any exception: lost without common carriage from 20 seats or 6,000 pounds.
notes.explanation: The air tour item sets its own seat and payload limits; the opening words of §119.1(e) apply to the whole list when common carriage is not involved.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 119.1 Applicability (eCFR), paragraph (e)(2)
notes.evidence: passenger-seat configuration of 30 seats or fewer and a maximum payload capacity of 7,500 pounds or less
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How does the carriage-for-hire ban for restricted category aircraft differ from that for experimental aircraft?
notes.back: Restricted: no carriage for hire at all, beyond its special purpose. Experimental: barred only in the listed operations, such as those needing part 119.
notes.explanation: The restricted rule is a flat ban with a special-purpose carve-out; the experimental rule works through a list.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.313 Restricted category civil aircraft: Operating limitations (eCFR), paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: No person may operate a restricted category civil aircraft carrying persons or property for compensation or hire. For the purposes of this paragraph (c), a special purpose operation
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force
